_doc: What Is a Ratio, Really? A concept explainer (about 3:54, one narrator, no characters). Voice: 'narrator' from audio/voices.example.json (a premade ElevenLabs voice). Colours: first amount = orange, second amount = green. Arc: screens hook (same shape, different sizes) -> for every (a ratio is a rule, not an amount) -> scaling by copying the group, ratio table, multiply both -> the tempting mistake (add the same) shown with rectangle shapes -> the line through zero (a ratio is a direction; 4:5 is off the line) -> unit rate by walking back the line -> part-to-whole (2 of every 5, not two thirds) -> recap + back to 16:9 -> your turn (10:15 yes, 5:6 no).

lines.text: {screens}A phone. {laptop}A laptop. {cinema}A cinema screen.
{sizes}Completely different sizes. {same}But look at their shape. It's the same.
{why}That's not a coincidence. They all share one thing: {ratio}a ratio. And once you really see what a ratio is, you'll start spotting them everywhere.
{tiles}Let's start small. Here are some tiles. {two}Two orange. {three}Three green.
{rule}A ratio is a rule that links two amounts. This one says: {forevery}for every two orange tiles, there are three green tiles.
{write}We write it like this. {r23}Two to three.
{notamount}Notice what a ratio doesn't tell you. It doesn't say how many tiles there are. {belong}It only says how the two amounts belong together.
{group}So let's treat those five tiles as one group. {copy}Now copy the group.
{r46}Four orange, six green. {samerule}Still two orange for every three green. {copy2}Again. {r69}Six and nine. {r812}Eight and twelve.
{table}Put them in a table, and a pattern appears. {times}To get from one row to another, both numbers are multiplied by the same number.
{equiv}These are all the same ratio. We call them equivalent ratios.
{tempt}But here's a question that trips up almost everyone. {why2}Why multiply? Why not add the same amount to both? {add}Two plus two, three plus two. {r45}Four to five. {fair}That feels fair.
{shape}Let's check, with shapes. {rect23}Draw a rectangle, two wide and three tall.
{rect46}Double both sides. Four by six. {bigger}It's bigger, but it's exactly the same shape.
{rect45}Now add two to both sides instead. Four by five. {squarer}Look. It's squarer. The shape has changed.
{diff}Adding keeps the difference the same. But a ratio isn't about the difference. {howmany}It's about how many times bigger one amount is than the other.

{plot}Here's the clearest way to see it. {axes}Put the orange amount across, and the green amount up. {pt23}Two and three is this point. {pt46}Four and six. {pt69}Six and nine. {pt812}Eight and twelve.
{line}They all sit on one straight line. {origin}And that line runs through zero.
{online}Every point on this line is the same ratio. {direction}A ratio is really a direction.
{pt45}And four to five? {off}It's off the line. Adding pushed it in a different direction.
{back}Now walk back along the line, all the way to one orange tile. {unitpt}There, you get one and a half green.

{unitrate}That's the unit rate. For every one, one and a half. {anyamount}With it, you can reach any point on the line. {five}Five orange? {fivex}Five times one and a half. {seven}Seven and a half green.
{total}A ratio also hides the whole. {of5}Two to three means that out of every five tiles, {twofifths}two are orange, {threefifths}and three are green.
{careful}So be careful. {nottwothirds}Two to three does not mean two thirds of the tiles are orange. {twooffive}It's two out of five.

{recap}So. {rec1}A ratio is a rule for how two amounts belong together. {rec2}Equivalent ratios come from multiplying both amounts by the same number, not adding. {rec3}And on a graph, they all lie on one line through zero.
{screens2}That's why every screen has the same shape. {sixteen}Sixteen to nine. {further}Every size is just a point further along the same line.
{tryq}Your turn. {q1}Is ten to fifteen the same ratio as two to three? {q2}And what about five to six?
{a1}Ten to fifteen: yes. It's two to three, times five. {a2}Five to six: no. That's three added to both, {offline}and it falls off the line.
